chunks: "I split it into dangers to people, to the equipment, and to the system around it.
For people, the main one is mechanical: a motor or solenoid can pinch, crush or entangle, and a modest servo with 20 kg·cm at a 2 cm lever pushes with nearly 100 newtons, plenty to hurt a finger.
Then unexpected motion, such as the MCU resetting or restarting after a fault. Heat is another: a stalled motor gets hot enough to burn.
Electrical shock matters for mains solenoids or high-voltage motors, and the inductive kick can be hundreds of volts even from a 12 volts coil.
A short in a battery-driven system can mean a fire. Strong magnets in motors can pinch and interfere with implants.
For equipment, inductive spikes kill MOSFETs, braking motors pump the supply voltage up, and stalls burn windings.
For the system, brushes arcing and PWM edges create EMI, and inrush makes the supply sag and resets controllers.

Mitigation: use the lowest voltage and power that works, guards and torque limits, fuses and current limits, a hardware e-stop that cuts power independent of firmware, flyback protection, gate pulldowns so the motor is off when the MCU is in reset, and fail-safe defaults so power loss leaves the load safe."
